sections.title: Dynamic systems in economic stabilization
teaching: A **dynamic system** changes over time as its parts influence one another. Woodford’s **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or DSGE, is the theory named in the economic example. Economics provides another setting for explaining fluctuations and considering how to reduce harmful extremes.

In the stabilization illustration, the **black curve represents unemployment** and the **gray curve inflation**. Large, jagged peaks and troughs become smaller and smoother. Stabilization means reducing those swings, rather than stopping all change or turning the two quantities into the same thing.

The connection with physical systems is the concern with what produces a fluctuation and what can reduce it. Here, the practical aim is to avoid extremes such as high unemployment or runaway inflation. The changing curves illustrate that aim without supplying a measured test of a particular policy.

sections.title: One mass, two directions
teaching: An **oscillation** is repeated movement around equilibrium, the resting position. A stretched or compressed spring pulls or pushes the mass back toward that position. The mass has **inertia**, so it keeps moving through equilibrium. The spring is then displaced the other way and brings it back again.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves across the spring line. The transverse segments are already pulled tight. Moving the mass above or below their resting line changes the direction of their pull, giving a force back toward the line.

The return force and the continued movement play different roles. If the mass is on one side of equilibrium, the spring acts toward equilibrium from that side. After the mass crosses, the spring’s displacement reverses and so does the restoring direction. The back-and-forth pattern comes from this repeated interaction, rather than from a force that always points the same way. The longitudinal and transverse pictures change how that return is arranged, while keeping the same basic relationship between movement and restoring action.

Both examples repeat at the same **frequency**, or number of cycles per unit of time, because their masses and total restoring stiffness are matched. Direction alone does not set the rate. These ideal examples have no damping, so the movement continues instead of gradually dying away.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Greater mass lowers frequency** when stiffness stays the same. A heavier mass is harder to speed up, slow down, and turn around. The same restoring action therefore takes longer to complete each back-and-forth cycle.

**Greater stiffness raises frequency** when mass stays the same. The same displacement produces a stronger force toward equilibrium, so the mass turns around more quickly and completes more cycles in the same time. Mass changes the resistance to changing motion; stiffness changes the strength of the return.

Each comparison keeps one property unchanged so that the cause of the rate change is clear. The heavier-mass example repeats the same kind of motion but completes fewer cycles than its reference. The stiffer example completes more. A larger visible movement would concern amplitude, or how far the mass travels, rather than establishing a faster rate. To identify frequency, follow complete repetitions over the same interval instead of judging which picture is tallest or which way the mass moves.

The longitudinal and transverse examples match within each comparison because their masses and **effective restoring stiffnesses** match. Effective stiffness means the restoring action in the actual direction of movement. Across the spring line, this depends on tension and arrangement. Making a spring harder to stretch along its length does not automatically increase its transverse restoring action.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Two equal masses connected between fixed ends have **two normal modes**. A normal mode is a coordinated pattern that repeats at one frequency, with the parts maintaining a particular relationship.

In **Mode 1**, both masses move in the same direction together. Their separation changes little, so the middle connection changes relatively little. In **Mode 2**, they move against each other, strongly compressing and stretching that connection. The stronger restoring action makes Mode 2 faster. Its frequency is higher, without necessarily being exactly twice Mode 1’s frequency.

In Mode 1, the masses can travel while keeping nearly the same distance between them. In Mode 2, their distance repeatedly shrinks and grows. That difference explains why the middle connection matters more in the faster pattern, even though the physical masses and connections have not been replaced. A mode describes the relationship across the whole system. It does not mean that one mass belongs to the first mode and the other belongs to the second; both masses participate in each pattern.

Both modes can contribute to the same masses at once. Their movements add at each mass, reinforcing in the same direction and canceling partly or completely in opposite directions. This addition is **superposition**. The combined motion contains both frequencies. The longitudinal and transverse versions preserve these relationships while changing the direction of movement.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal masses between fixed ends have **three normal modes**. In **Mode 1**, all move in the same direction, but the middle mass moves farthest. Moving together therefore does not require equal distances. This is the lowest-frequency pattern.

In **Mode 2**, the outer masses move oppositely while the middle mass stays at equilibrium because the pulls on it balance. That stationary location is a **node**. In **Mode 3**, the outer masses move together against the middle mass. Neighboring parts oppose one another more strongly, making this the fastest pattern.

The order follows how the masses move relative to their neighbors. Mode 1 keeps their broad movement together. Mode 2 makes the outer masses oppose one another but leaves the middle balanced. Mode 3 makes the middle oppose both outer masses, strongly changing their connecting links. These are different arrangements of movement in the same system, not a progression in which an extra mass starts moving at each stage. The colors track the individual masses and the resting marks show what each displacement is measured from.

The frequencies belong to this chain and are not necessarily one, two, and three times the lowest. When the modes combine, their movements add at each mass. The center can move through contributions from Modes 1 and 3 even though it is a node in Mode 2. The same relationships appear in the matched longitudinal and transverse models.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: Each movable mass adds one independent **normal mode** in the direction being modeled. The chains with one through six masses therefore have one through six modes. The empty spaces mark modes that smaller chains do not have, giving 21 displayed comparisons altogether.

Within a chain, **Mode 1** has the broadest pattern, with the masses moving together. Higher modes introduce more groups moving in opposite directions. The connections undergo stronger relative changes, and the patterns repeat faster. Fixed endpoints remain still; a stationary mass inside one mode does not mean the whole chain has stopped.

Within each chain, the masses and connections are equal and both outer supports remain fixed. Changing the mode changes how those same parts move in relation to one another. A higher pattern has more reversals across the chain, so neighboring parts pull against one another in more places. This explains the faster restoring pattern without claiming that a higher mode uses smaller masses or physically stronger replacement springs. Mode number identifies the pattern, not the identity of a particular moving mass.

Colors identify mode number, while each row identifies the number of masses. The largest movements are scaled to the same displayed size, so height cannot establish which mode is faster. **Amplitude** is movement size; frequency is repetition rate. These separate-mass chains generally lack the exact whole-number frequency spacing of an ideal continuous string.
concepts: one additional mass gives one additional mode

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A **fixed–fixed string** stays still at both endpoints, which are nodes. Mode 1 fits one half-wave into its length; Modes 2–5 fit two through five. More half-waves mean shorter wavelengths and faster repetition at the same wave speed. These frequencies are consecutive **harmonics**, including odd and even multiples of the fundamental.

The same string can contain all five modes. Their movements add at each position, reinforcing or canceling as their cycles progress. The combined outline changes even though the component patterns remain regular. Playback slows all modes equally, preserving their relative rates.

The displayed components are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz. These labels identify their repetition rates, whereas the half-wave count identifies their shapes along the string. As the mixture moves, a position can become nearly flat through cancellation and later move strongly as the contributions change. This does not mean that a component frequency has been destroyed and replaced. The measured motion still combines the original patterns, with each contribution depending on how that particular mode moves the pickup location.

The marked **pickup** measures movement at one point. Its spectrum places frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically. The five peaks correspond to the five components. Their heights are equal because the mode strengths were chosen to give equal contributions at this pickup; another position can give different heights. Equal peaks do not mean equal movement everywhere.
concepts: integer harmonics including odd and even

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: **Increasing mass lowers frequency** when stiffness is unchanged, because the moving load becomes harder to turn around. **Increasing stiffness raises frequency** when mass is unchanged, because the stronger restoring force changes the movement more quickly.

Location matters within a larger system. Added mass strongly affects a mode where the material moves a lot. Extra stiffness matters where neighboring parts stretch or compress strongly. Neighbors can travel together without greatly changing their separation, so strong movement and strong compression are different. Their largest regions alternate in these ideal patterns.

A normal mode is a coordinated movement that repeats at one frequency. Its parts can move different distances or in opposite directions while still belonging to that pattern. A local change therefore has to be compared with the whole mode’s shape. The same added mass can be important where one mode moves strongly and relatively unimportant where another hardly moves. A point that is a node in one pattern is not necessarily stationary in other patterns or in their combined movement.

Each movable mass supplies one independent chain mode, generally without exact harmonic spacing. Endpoint conditions select different continuous patterns: fixed–fixed systems fit whole half-waves; fixed–free systems fit odd quarter-waves. The mode’s shape and the changed region together determine how strongly a local mass or stiffness change affects its frequency.
concepts: different roles of one region across modes

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently
teaching: The highlighted region lies left of the string’s midpoint. **Mode 4** moves that region strongly, with neighboring positions traveling similarly. **Mode 5** has relatively little movement there but stronger local stretching and compression because neighboring positions move differently.

Adding **mass** strongly slows Mode 4 because its movement has to carry the extra load. The same mass change matters less to Mode 5, which hardly moves the region. This concerns movement over a cycle, rather than whether one still frame happens to catch a point at rest.

Increasing **stiffness** matters more to Mode 5 because it strongly stretches the region, adding restoring action and raising its frequency. Mode 4 stretches it less, so the stiffness effect is smaller. If mass and stiffness both increase there, the main prediction is **Mode 4 lower and Mode 5 higher**. The same location has different roles in the two patterns.
concepts: movement over a cycle versus momentary rest

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** moves across a surface with fixed outside edges. Its two-number labels count moving regions along the two surface directions. (1,1) has one broad region; (2,1) and (1,2) divide it in different directions; (2,2) makes four regions; and (3,1) makes three along one direction. Neighboring regions move oppositely, separated by stationary nodes.

The five movements add at every point. Contributions can reinforce or cancel, producing one changing surface. The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale, so its apparent height cannot be compared directly with the individual panels.

A node stays still throughout that mode’s cycle. A moving region can also pass briefly through the resting surface, but that momentary crossing does not make it a node. The distinction matters when reading an animation from one frame. Follow the same region as it rises, crosses rest, and falls while its neighbor moves oppositely. The two numbers describe divisions across the surface, rather than two separate frequencies, two different membranes, or a count of cycles that have already elapsed.

The pickup records one location. The spectrum gives frequency horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The component strengths were chosen to make equal peaks there. Frequencies of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz were **assigned for the illustration**, rather than calculated as this rectangle’s natural resonances. Their equal spacing demonstrates combining frequencies; it does not establish that every membrane naturally has harmonic spacing.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **scientific theory** explains a system precisely enough to make a testable prediction. Differential equations describe how its quantities change. Their purpose here is to connect the proposed mechanism with an observable result, rather than to provide a calculation exercise.

The proposed theory treats the **vocal folds as a vibrating membrane**. It predicts **equidistant harmonics** in a laryngeal vibration signal: frequency peaks separated by equal intervals. Testing it requires recording actual laryngeal vibration and examining its spectrum. Regular spacing would agree with the prediction; a different pattern would question the model’s account of that signal.

The proposed observation is more specific than simply seeing movement. The vocal folds could vibrate while the measured frequencies fail to follow the predicted equal spacing. Examining the spectrum connects the theory with the particular feature it predicts. The animation demonstrates what an assigned collection of frequencies looks like when combined; a recording asks whether an actual vocal-fold signal has the proposed pattern. Keeping those roles separate distinguishes an illustration of an idea from evidence obtained by testing that idea.

The material proposes this experiment without reporting a measured outcome. The membrane animation uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so replaying that illustration is not an independent test of natural vocal-fold vibration.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed–free system** must have a node at the fixed end and an **antinode**, a place of maximum movement, at the free end. The simplest pattern fits one quarter-wave. The next patterns fit three, five, and seven quarter-waves, giving the first, third, fifth, and seventh harmonics. Mode 2 is therefore the third harmonic, not the second.

Odd quarter-wave counts preserve the different endpoint conditions. Even counts would put a node at the free end. Higher patterns fit shorter wavelengths into the same length and repeat faster. The mixture’s spectrum gives frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically. Equal excitation produces equal peaks at the free-end pickup; uniformly slowed playback preserves the relative rates.

An antinode is a place with the greatest movement over a cycle, not a point that stays at its farthest position. It passes through rest and moves to the other side while the fixed endpoint remains still. The illustrated frequencies are 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. The second, third, and fourth allowed modes are consequently the third, fifth, and seventh harmonics. Counting allowed shapes and comparing their frequencies answer different questions, even though both descriptions use numbers.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **separately tuned** to the same fundamental. Changing only one endpoint while keeping length and wave speed unchanged would halve the fundamental. Matching displayed labels therefore does not isolate the endpoint’s effect.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air has **inertia**, so moving air tends to keep moving. Compression produces a restoring effect, represented by the model’s spring-like links. The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, rather than traveling steadily from the glottis to the lips.

The glottal end is treated as fixed and the open lips as free. **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the lowest resonance pattern; **Mode 2 is F2-like**, with another internal reversal. In the ideal uniform reference, Mode 2 repeats three times as fast. A changed tract shape can alter that simple relationship.

A resonance pattern describes the air system’s coordinated back-and-forth movement. F1 and F2 do not identify two separate streams or two positions from which sound is emitted. At one location, neighboring elements may move together while their gaps hardly change. At another, the gaps may repeatedly close and open. A constriction acts on both modes at the same physical place, but their different movement and compression patterns give the changed region a different role in each.

The /a/ marker is about one-third of the distance from the glottis, /i/ about two-thirds, and /u/ at the lips. Each marks the same place in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly; increased springiness matters where it compresses strongly. Comparing these local roles explains why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.
concepts: simplified glottal fixed and lip free boundaries

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: **Tongue height** and **front–back position** describe vowel articulation. The vowel in **dean** is high and front, with its marked narrowing about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. **Dune** is high and back, with a highlighted narrowing at the lips. Sharing tongue height does not give them the same tract shape.

**Dan** is low and front; **Don** is low and back, with its narrowing marked about one-third of the distance from the glottis. **Done** is central and labeled “No constriction,” providing the relatively unconstricted reference. Dan has no numbered narrowing position.

The labels describe related but different features. High versus low concerns tongue height; front versus back concerns its position along the mouth; the marked fraction concerns distance along the air path. A shared label such as high therefore leaves other shape differences open. Dean and dune can both be high while narrowing different places, and those places can play different roles in the second resonance pattern. Describing articulation identifies what changed physically; comparing the air modes explains what that change does to the sound.

These fractions locate changes along the air passage, starting at the glottis. A narrowing changes the local mass-like and spring-like effects. Its acoustic consequence depends on how each mode moves and compresses that region, connecting vowel shape with the direction of a formant change.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end
teaching: The **/u/ model** adds loading near the open lips, the free end of the air column. Both the F1-like and F2-like patterns have substantial movement there. The enlarged elements represent greater **effective mass**, not heavier individual air molecules.

More moving mass is harder to speed up and reverse. Where this effect dominates, each cycle takes longer and frequency falls. Because both modes move strongly near the lips, the result is **F1 down and F2 down** relative to the uniform reference.

The two rows make it possible to compare the same lip location across different resonance patterns. Both have strong movement there, even though their internal arrangements differ. Increasing the load therefore slows both without requiring that their shapes or frequencies become identical. F1 remains the lower resonance and F2 the next one. The important comparison is the direction of each change relative to its own uniform reference, not whether the two frequencies have become equal or whether all parts of the tract move equally.

The shared direction follows from the changed location’s role in both patterns. It is not a rule that every constriction lowers every resonance. The air continues moving back and forth around its usual positions; the larger elements identify the load involved in that movement.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The **/i/ constriction** lies near the front, about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. It changes the same physical region in both modes, but that region contributes differently to their movement and compression.

For **Mode 1**, movement makes the **mass effect** more important. The extra effective load is harder to reverse, slowing the cycle and lowering F1. For **Mode 2**, compression makes the **springiness effect** more important. A stronger restoring response speeds the cycle and raises F2.

The marked region is not moved to a new location when the mode changes. What changes is the role of that same region within the coordinated movement. Neighbors moving together make extra moving load important; neighbors repeatedly approaching and separating make the restoring response important. Comparing both rows prevents the narrowing from being treated as a single instruction to raise or lower every frequency. The two arrows summarize separate causal explanations, one involving slower movement of added mass and the other a faster return from compression.

The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** relative to the uniform reference. Increasing mass-like and spring-like effects together does not mean they cancel. Their importance depends on how each mode uses the narrowed region, so one constriction can move the two resonances in opposite directions.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects
teaching: The **/a/ constriction** lies farther back, about one-third of the way from the glottis to the lips. This changes a different part of each mode from the front /i/ narrowing, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness remain the same.

For **Mode 1**, compression is important at the changed region. Greater springiness supplies a stronger restoring response, making the cycle faster and raising F1. For **Mode 2**, movement matters more there. Greater effective mass makes the moving air harder to reverse, slowing the cycle and lowering F2.

The narrowing affects the same back location in both rows, but the rows describe different coordinated movements of the air. A region can have little movement of its own while its neighbors repeatedly squeeze together and spread apart. It can also move strongly with relatively little spacing change. Those two roles explain why the spring-like effect dominates the first mode here while the moving-load effect dominates the second. Changing constriction location changes which role is most important; it does not change what mass or stiffness means.

The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, reversing the /i/ pattern. The explanation connects constriction location with local movement or compression, then with the effect on frequency. The directions describe the model’s predicted change rather than numerical measurements of its size.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: **Air movement** concerns how far an element travels; **compression** concerns changes in the gaps between neighbors. Elements can travel together with little change in spacing. Elsewhere, neighbors can approach and separate strongly around a point whose own movement is small. Smaller gaps mean compression, while wider gaps mean rarefaction, or more spread-out air.

The moving **Schwa** row supplies the uniform-tube reference. The F1, F2, and F3 rows separate resonance patterns of that same air column. The closed left end restricts movement and the open right end allows it. Higher modes fit more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

Compression changes supply a restoring response because crowded air pushes back toward its usual spacing. The moving air also has inertia, so it continues moving as that restoring response changes. Together they support repeated motion around the usual positions. A region with large movement can carry substantial moving mass without being the region that squeezes most strongly. A region with large spacing changes can supply strong restoring action without its central element traveling far. These observations connect the visible circles and gaps with the mass-and-spring explanation.

Following an element over a cycle reveals movement; following neighboring gaps reveals compression. Added mass matters most where movement is strong, while added stiffness matters most where compression changes strongly. These locations differ between modes. The rows represent different resonances, not separate air streams.
concepts: multiple resonances in one air system
